The radar absorbing material (RAM) designed has a thickness of 6.25 mm and achieves more than -10 dB reflection loss from 4 to 18 GHz.
Three rivet configurations were studied: RAS C1 (center of unit cell), RAS C2 (between two unit cells), and RAS C3 (center of four unit cells).
Rivet head surface area percentages relative to RAS surface area were 9.8%, 4.4%, and 2.5%.
Rivet surface area of 9.8% caused up to 10 dB degradation in reflection coefficient and mono-static RCS.
Reducing rivet surface area to 4.4% and 2.5% reduced RCS degradation to approximately 5 dB and 3 dB respectively.
Longer air intake ducts (up to 8 meters) showed improved RCS performance compared to shorter ducts.
Simulations covered frequencies from 1 to 30 GHz for flat panels and 1 to 18 GHz for air intake ducts and aircraft models.
Mono-static RCS was evaluated for incident angles ϴ=0° and azimuth ϕ varying from -90° to +90° or 180° to 270° depending on the case.
The presence of rivets degrades RCS performance, but RAS air intake ducts still provide significant RCS reduction compared to metallic ducts.
The open-source aircraft CAD model showed about 10 dB RCS reduction with RAS air intake ducts compared to non-RAS ducts.
Rivet installation location affects RCS degradation, with RAS C1 configuration showing the worst impact.
Both horizontal (HH) and vertical (VV) polarizations were analyzed, showing similar trends in RCS degradation.
The study used full-wave Floquet port analysis and high-frequency shooting and bouncing rays methods for electromagnetic simulations.
Weak scatterers like fasteners are critical contributors to RCS in stealth aircraft and must be carefully analyzed.
The RAM design uses a Jerusalem cross unit cell embedded in FR4 material with dielectric constant 4.4 and loss tangent 0.02.
The rivet diameter considered was 4.0 mm with a 90° countersunk head.
The RAS performance degrades below 4 GHz due to design limitations of the RAM.
The study highlights that external aircraft shape also influences overall RCS but was not addressed here.
The RCS degradation due to rivets is frequency-dependent and varies across the 4 to 18 GHz band.
The study is the first reported evaluation of rivet impact on RAS air intake duct RCS performance.
